We are writing a literature review to discover which tests determine the value of a robot arm used as an automated manual manipulator in a self-driving laboratory (SDL) for materials science. By automated manual manipulator we mean one arm that does the hands-on work a person would otherwise do: it moves from station to station (for example a pipetting gantry, a powder doser, a balance, vial and plate racks), recalibrates itself at each station using a calibration square (a square fiducial target such as an AprilTag, or a square fixture at a known position), and takes on several new automated tasks. The term is ours; the literature may say mobile manipulator, robotic laboratory assistant, robot chemist, or sample- or labware-handling robot. Our arms are a low-cost AgileX PiPER 6-DOF arm (about $2k) and SO-101 leader/follower arms (about $200), with parallel grippers, Raspberry Pi wrist cameras and fixed cameras in an enclosure, AprilTags, and LeRobot-style imitation learning or scripted motion. We want to place these arms in the published literature and find tests that we, or anyone validating an affordable arm, can repeat to compare it with the industry-standard arms used in SDLs (e.g. UR5e, UR3, Franka Panda, ABB YuMi, Kinova, KUKA), including on cost per task.

Station-to-station calibration: What published systems have one robot arm (on a mobile base, on a rail or fixed) move between laboratory stations and recalibrate or re-localize itself at each station against a calibration target, such as a cube or square fixture probed by touch, an AprilTag, ArUco or other square fiducial, or a checkerboard (as in the mobile robotic chemist)? For each, what positioning accuracy was reached after calibration, how was it measured (protocol, number of trials, measuring tool), how long did calibration take, and what tolerance did the station tasks need? Describe tests that could check station-to-station calibration on a low-cost arm, and how accurately AprilTags or wrist cameras localize at working distances.

Prioritize peer-reviewed journal articles and major conference papers from 2015 to 2026, and flag any preprints. For each benchmark or result, describe the protocol in enough detail to repeat it (what is measured, number of trials, success criterion, measuring tool) and give the arm model. For each claim, give the DOI and quote the sentence that supports it. Say explicitly where no published evidence exists.

# Station-to-Station Calibration of Robot Arms in Self-Driving Laboratories: A Literature Review

## 1. Introduction

This review identifies published systems in which a single robot arm moves between laboratory stations and recalibrates at each one, the positioning accuracy achieved, the protocols used to measure it, and the tolerances required by downstream tasks. It then synthesizes these findings into a set of repeatable tests suitable for validating low-cost arms such as the AgileX PiPER (~$2k) and SO-101 leader/follower arms (~$200) against industry-standard platforms (KUKA iiwa, UR5e, Franka Panda, etc.) used in self-driving laboratories (SDLs).

## 2. Published Systems with Station-to-Station Recalibration

The following table summarizes all systems identified in the literature where a robot arm navigates or is repositioned between stations and recalibrates against a local target.

### 2.1 The Mobile Robotic Chemist (Burger et al., 2020)

The foundational SDL mobile manipulator is the KUKA KMR system described by Burger et al. (2020, *Nature*). The robot uses a KUKA LBR iiwa 7-DOF arm on an omnidirectional mobile platform that navigates a 7.3 × 11 m laboratory using laser scanning. At each station, it performs a **six-point (6P) touch calibration** against a rigid rectangular cube (100 × 100 × 50 mm). Three contact points define one plane, two define a perpendicular plane, and one defines the third, establishing the cube's coordinate frame relative to the robot (burger2023amobilerobotic pages 52-56). Testing with 100 separate calibrations, with initial-position noise of up to ±15 mm in x/y and ±2.5° in orientation, showed that "the cube was recovered within 0.12 mm, while orientation offsets were reduced to less than 0.005°" (burger2023amobilerobotic pages 52-56). The robot achieved "an x–y positioning precision of ±0.12 mm and an orientation precision of ±0.005 degrees" enabling manipulations comparable to human researchers (burger2020amobilerobotic pages 1-3). No vision system was used; the robot operated using laser scanning and touch feedback, allowing operation in complete darkness (burger2020amobilerobotic pages 1-3). The robustness test required "navigation to the station followed by 6P calibration before manipulation" at every iteration (burger2023amobilerobotic pages 62-69). DOI: 10.1038/s41586-020-2442-2.

### 2.2 LIRA: Vision-Based ArUco Localization (Zhou et al., 2025)

Zhou et al. (2025, *Communications Chemistry*) introduced LIRA, which replaces the tactile 6P method with ArUco fiducial markers mounted on laboratory instruments. The evaluation protocol defined a reference position 300 mm from the calibration marker; the robot was commanded to that position after each calibration, and "translational and rotational deviations were calculated, and the procedure was repeated 100 times for statistical reliability" (zhou2025localizationinspectionand pages 2-3). Key results: a 20 mm ArUco marker without filtering produced 2.42 mm mean translational error and 3.46° rotational error; with Gaussian and mean filtering this improved to 1.51 mm and 1.54°; a 75 mm marker yielded 1.02 mm and 1.01°; and the tactile cube comparator achieved 0.92 mm and 0.90° (zhou2025localizationinspectionand pages 3-5). Critically, visual calibration took approximately 5 seconds per station versus approximately 53 seconds for the tactile method, and "LIRA reduced total arm-manipulation time by 36.1% (873 seconds versus 1367 seconds)" (zhou2025localizationinspectionand pages 7-8). DOI: 10.1038/s42004-025-01770-1.

### 2.3 Mobile Robotic Process Chemist (Brass et al., 2026 — Preprint)

Brass et al. (2026, *ChemRxiv* preprint) describe a mobile robot that works between a fume hood, filtration system, weighing station, and UHPLC-MS. The system "used visual fiducial markers to compensate for mobile-base positioning errors and to localize the robot end effector," replacing the earlier 6P method and achieving "±0.41 mm translation precision and ±1.014° rotational precision" (brass2026amobilerobotic pages 7-10). The specific fiducial marker type and size are not reported in the extracted text. DOI: 10.26434/chemrxiv-2025-bsfvz.

### 2.4 Manufacturing Mobile Manipulator with AprilTag Docking (Bavelos et al., 2021)

In a manufacturing analogue directly relevant to SDL station-to-station workflows, Bavelos et al. (2021, *Applied Sciences*) describe an omnidirectional mobile manipulator that navigates between workstations, then performs "virtual docking" using fiducial markers (AprilTag and Alvar families tested). A stereo Intel RealSense camera detects the marker, establishes the station reference frame, and a "closed-loop PID controller then commands the omnidirectional wheels until the error reaches an acceptable threshold, achieving a maximum localization error of 1 cm" (bavelos2021enablingflexibilityin pages 7-9). This demonstrates the general pattern: coarse navigation followed by vision-based fine re-localization against a station fiducial. DOI: 10.3390/app11093985.

### 2.5 Other SDL Systems

**Sulaiman et al. (2026)** describe a UR5e on a Clearpath Ridgeback omnidirectional base for SDL operations, using SIFT/FLANN/RANSAC-based vision for object localization, though no numerical station-calibration accuracy is reported (sulaiman2026kinematicanalysisand pages 6-9, sulaiman2026kinematicanalysisand pages 3-6). DOI: 10.1007/s41315-025-00518-3.

**Dai et al. (2024, *Nature*)** extend the Cooper group's mobile robot approach to exploratory synthetic chemistry with multiple mobile robots sharing equipment with human researchers, but the extracted text does not provide calibration accuracy numbers. DOI: 10.1038/s41586-024-08173-7.

**Self-Building Labs (Bai et al., 2026 — preprint)** use wrist-mounted cameras and iterative digital-twin refinement to establish robot-to-device transforms, noting that "grasping and insertion require millimetre-scale precision" (bai2026selfbuildinglabs pages 4-7). DOI: 10.48550/arxiv.2610.23826.

## 3. AprilTag and ArUco Localization Accuracy at Working Distances

The table separates mean error, maximum error, RMSE, and systematic bias because these metrics are not directly interchangeable.*

Key findings:

- **Close range, filtered, controlled conditions (LIRA):** A 75 mm ArUco marker at ~300 mm yields 1.02 mm mean translational error and 1.01° rotational error over 100 trials, approaching the 0.92 mm tactile reference (zhou2025localizationinspectionand pages 3-5).
- **Close range, robotic arm (Franchini et al., 2023):** AprilTag/TagSLAM at <1 m achieves "translational positioning accuracy better than 1 cm" and "rotational accuracy better than 0.5 degrees" (franchini2023mechatronicdesignand pages 6-7). DOI: 10.1109/metroaerospace57412.2023.10190044.
- **Hand-camera bias (Wilcock & Iuorio, 2026):** An end-effector-mounted camera showed a mean distance bias of +14 mm for AprilTag, versus +69 mm for a tripod-mounted global camera (wilcock2026fusionoffiducial pages 8-9). DOI: 10.1007/s41693-026-00183-3.
- **Marker size matters:** Yu et al. (2021) showed AprilTag mean Euclidean error decreasing from 41.8 mm (67.5 mm marker) to 17.8 mm (126 mm marker), and ArUco error decreasing from 62.0 mm to 7.0 mm across corresponding sizes (yu2021applicationofa pages 16-18). Camera resolution also matters: at 2048×2048 pixels, AprilTag relative error dropped to 0.18% mean (yu2021applicationofa pages 16-18). DOI: 10.3390/s21051829.
- **Dynamic conditions degrade accuracy severely:** Lvov et al. (2023) report AprilTag RMSE of 5.11 cm static at 0.9 m, worsening to 8.86–9.16 cm under angular motion at 1 m (lvov2023mobilemocapretroreflector pages 4-5, lvov2023mobilemocapretroreflector pages 5-6). DOI: 10.1109/case56687.2023.10260562.

**Practical implication for low-cost arms:** At typical wrist-camera working distances of 0.2–0.4 m, with a 50–75 mm AprilTag, a Raspberry Pi camera at ≥1280×960 resolution, and temporal filtering (median of N frames), sub-5 mm translational accuracy is achievable. This is sufficient for vial handling (tolerances ~2 mm) but may be marginal for microplate seating without mechanical compliance aids.

## 4. Benchmarks for Robot Arm Accuracy in Laboratory Automation

### 4.1 Microplate Handling Repeatability (Harazono et al., 2024 — Preprint)

Harazono et al. constructed a reusable platform with dial gauges to measure microplate transfer repeatability on a Dobot M1 Pro SCARA arm. At 100% speed over 125 transfers, the interquartile range was "0.020 mm in x and 0.006 mm in y," while at 50% speed it was "0.034 mm in x and 0.014 mm in y" (harazono2024evaluationofmicroplate pages 11-15). Lid-placement success "declined sharply above Δy = 2.190 mm" (harazono2024evaluationofmicroplate pages 11-15). The study emphasizes that "repeatability can be affected by the payload, attached end effector, and temperature-related drift, and that manufacturer repeatability specifications may not represent actual loaded microplate handling" (harazono2024evaluationofmicroplate pages 1-6). DOI: 10.1101/2023.12.29.573685.

### 4.2 REPLAB: Low-Cost Arm Benchmark (~$2,000)

Yang et al. (2019, ICRA) introduced REPLAB, a standardized ~$2,000 work cell with an Interbotix WidowX 6-DOF arm. Calibration uses a checkerboard for camera registration and a 5×5 floor grid to fit an affine correction model (q = αp + β). "End-effector positions were within 2 cm of targets across the 35×40 cm workspace and within 1 cm near its center" (yang2019replabareproducible pages 2-3, yang2019replabareproduciblea pages 2-3). The benchmark includes >50,000 grasp attempts with standardized task definitions, evaluation protocols, and performance measures (yang2019replabareproduciblea pages 1-2). DOI: 10.1109/ICRA.2019.8794390.

### 4.3 Nanoparticle Synthesis Platform (Dembski et al., 2023)

Dembski et al. used a dual-arm Yaskawa MOTOMAN CSDA10F for automated nanoparticle synthesis, benchmarking against three laboratory technicians each performing triplicate measurements. "Automated dosing achieved relatively small deviations and was reported to be at least as accurate as manual dosing" with "personnel costs estimated to decrease by 75% per synthesis" (dembski2023establishingandtesting pages 6-7, dembski2023establishingandtesting pages 3-6). DOI: 10.1038/s41598-023-38535-6.

### 4.4 OSCAR: Open-Source Lab Robot with UR3

The OSCAR platform uses a UR3 arm (academic price ~CAD 25,000) with a Robotiq 2F-140 gripper, force-torque sensor, and Intel RealSense D415 camera. The authors note that "calibration is required for high-Cartesian-accuracy tasks such as pipet-tip attachment and colony picking" and that "robust calibration can take a few hours through trial-and-error" (pivin2026oscaramodular pages 9-10). DOI: 10.1021/acssynbio.5c00733.

## 5. Low-Cost Arms and Imitation Learning for Laboratory Tasks

### 5.1 SO-101 with ACT/LeRobot for Vial Handling (Johns & Gongora, 2026)

The most directly relevant work for the user's configuration is Johns and Gongora (2026), who used an SO-101 6-DOF leader/follower arm with a custom cylindrical-fit gripper and two RGB cameras, trained using the LeRobot framework. For laboratory vial handling, "the ACT policy achieved 34 successful placements in 36 fixed-start physical trials, corresponding to a 94.4% task success rate" while "SmolVLA achieved 31/36 successes (91.1%)" (johns2026towardautonomousrobots pages 5-8, johns2026towardautonomousrobots pages 8-9). Key design insights included that "a 45-degree oblique camera view was found preferable to a top-down view because it preserved depth, contact, height, tilt, and alignment cues" (johns2026towardautonomousrobots pages 5-8). No formal geometric calibration protocol or positioning accuracy measurement was reported; reliability came from closed-loop visual policies and mechanical gripper design rather than kinematic precision (johns2026towardautonomousrobots pages 1-5). DOI: 10.2172/3684119.

### 5.2 Placing PiPER and SO-101 in Context

**No published work was found on the AgileX PiPER arm in SDL or laboratory contexts.** The SO-101 appears only in the Johns & Gongora report. For comparison: REPLAB's WidowX arm (~$2,000) achieved ~2 cm position accuracy with open-loop commands (yang2019replabareproducible pages 2-3); industry-standard arms achieve 0.01–0.1 mm repeatability (manufacturer specifications for UR5e: ±0.03 mm; KUKA iiwa: ±0.1 mm); and the LIRA system shows that vision-based correction with ArUco markers can bring effective accuracy to ~1 mm regardless of the underlying arm kinematic error (zhou2025localizationinspectionand pages 3-5).

## 6. Where No Published Evidence Exists

Several gaps in the literature should be noted explicitly:

1. **No published station-to-station calibration test has been performed on any arm costing less than ~$2,000.** The REPLAB benchmark evaluates grasping but not station recalibration. Johns & Gongora evaluate task success but not calibration accuracy.
2. **No published work reports AprilTag or ArUco localization accuracy specifically from a Raspberry Pi camera at robot-arm working distances (0.2–0.4 m).** The LIRA results use an unspecified camera; Franchini et al. do not specify camera model; published Raspberry Pi camera evaluations are from UAV contexts at longer ranges.
3. **No published cost-per-task metric exists for SDL robot arms.** Dembski et al. report 75% personnel cost reduction but not cost per successful manipulation. No study compares amortized hardware cost per task across arm price tiers.
4. **No published protocol combines station-to-station navigation, visual recalibration, and manipulation success into a single repeatable benchmark for any arm class.**
5. **Calibration time is rarely reported.** Only LIRA provides a direct comparison (~5 s visual vs. ~53 s tactile per calibration) (zhou2025localizationinspectionand pages 7-8).

## 7. Recommended Tests for Validating a Low-Cost Arm

It separates calibration accuracy, loaded repeatability, task success, cycle reliability, timing, and cost so that results are reproducible and failure modes remain visible.*

## 8. Summary and Recommendations

The literature on station-to-station calibration in SDLs is dominated by the Cooper group's KUKA-based mobile robotic chemist and its successors. The progression from tactile 6P calibration (±0.12 mm, ~53 s) to ArUco vision-based calibration (1.02 mm with 75 mm markers, ~5 s) demonstrates that visual fiducial calibration is now competitive with touch-based methods for most SDL tasks (zhou2025localizationinspectionand pages 3-5, zhou2025localizationinspectionand pages 7-8). For a low-cost arm like the PiPER or SO-101, the most promising approach is to combine AprilTag-based station re-localization (using markers ≥50 mm at ≤400 mm distance with temporal filtering) with closed-loop imitation learning policies that compensate for residual kinematic errors through visual feedback, as demonstrated by Johns & Gongora's 94.4% vial-placement success rate on the SO-101 (johns2026towardautonomousrobots pages 5-8).

The critical missing piece is a published, repeatable benchmark that integrates station-to-station navigation, fiducial recalibration, and task success into a single protocol applicable across arm price tiers. The seven-test suite proposed in this review is designed to fill that gap.

# Station-to-Station Calibration of Robot Arms in Self-Driving Laboratories: A Literature Review

## 1. Introduction

This review identifies published systems in which a single robot arm moves between laboratory stations and recalibrates at each one, the positioning accuracy achieved, the protocols used to measure it, and the tolerances required by downstream tasks. It then synthesizes these findings into a set of repeatable tests suitable for validating low-cost arms such as the AgileX PiPER (~$2k) and SO-101 leader/follower arms (~$200) against industry-standard platforms (KUKA iiwa, UR5e, Franka Panda, etc.) used in self-driving laboratories (SDLs).

## 2. Published Systems with Station-to-Station Recalibration

### 2.1 The Mobile Robotic Chemist (Burger et al., 2020)

The foundational SDL mobile manipulator is the KUKA KMR system described by Burger et al. (2020, *Nature*). The robot uses a KUKA LBR iiwa 7-DOF arm on an omnidirectional mobile platform that navigates a 7.3 × 11 m laboratory using laser scanning. At each station, it performs a **six-point (6P) touch calibration** against a rigid rectangular cube (100 × 100 × 50 mm). Three contact points define one plane, two define a perpendicular plane, and one defines the third, establishing the cube's coordinate frame relative to the robot (pqac-00000000, pqac-00000013). Testing with 100 separate calibrations, with initial-position noise of up to ±15 mm in x/y and ±2.5° in orientation, showed that "the cube was recovered within 0.12 mm, while orientation offsets were reduced to less than 0.005°" (pqac-00000000). The robot achieved "an x–y positioning precision of ±0.12 mm and an orientation precision of ±0.005 degrees" enabling manipulations comparable to human researchers (pqac-00000002). No vision system was used; the robot operated using laser scanning and touch feedback, allowing operation in complete darkness (pqac-00000002). The robustness test required "navigation to the station followed by 6P calibration before manipulation" at every iteration (pqac-00000001). DOI: 10.1038/s41586-020-2442-2.

### 2.2 LIRA: Vision-Based ArUco Localization (Zhou et al., 2025)

Zhou et al. (2025, *Communications Chemistry*) introduced LIRA, which replaces the tactile 6P method with ArUco fiducial markers mounted on laboratory instruments. The evaluation protocol defined a reference position 300 mm from the calibration marker; the robot was commanded to that position after each calibration, and "translational and rotational deviations were calculated, and the procedure was repeated 100 times for statistical reliability" (pqac-00000004, pqac-00000008). Key results: a 20 mm ArUco marker without filtering produced 2.42 mm mean translational error and 3.46° rotational error; with Gaussian and mean filtering this improved to 1.51 mm and 1.54°; a 75 mm marker yielded 1.02 mm and 1.01°; and the tactile cube comparator achieved 0.92 mm and 0.90° (pqac-00000005). Critically, visual calibration took approximately 5 seconds per station versus approximately 53 seconds for the tactile method, and "LIRA reduced total arm-manipulation time by 36.1% (873 seconds versus 1367 seconds)" (pqac-00000006). DOI: 10.1038/s42004-025-01770-1.

### 2.3 Mobile Robotic Process Chemist (Brass et al., 2026 — Preprint)

Brass et al. (2026, *ChemRxiv* preprint) describe a mobile robot that works between a fume hood, filtration system, weighing station, and UHPLC-MS. The system "used visual fiducial markers to compensate for mobile-base positioning errors and to localize the robot end effector," replacing the earlier 6P method and achieving "±0.41 mm translation precision and ±1.014° rotational precision" (pqac-00000020). The specific fiducial marker type and size are not reported in the extracted text. DOI: 10.26434/chemrxiv-2025-bsfvz.

### 2.4 Manufacturing Mobile Manipulator with AprilTag Docking (Bavelos et al., 2021)

In a manufacturing analogue directly relevant to SDL station-to-station workflows, Bavelos et al. (2021, *Applied Sciences*) describe an omnidirectional mobile manipulator that navigates between workstations, then performs "virtual docking" using fiducial markers (AprilTag and Alvar families tested). A stereo Intel RealSense camera detects the marker, establishes the station reference frame, and a "closed-loop PID controller then commands the omnidirectional wheels until the error reaches an acceptable threshold, achieving a maximum localization error of 1 cm" (pqac-00000042). This demonstrates the general pattern: coarse navigation followed by vision-based fine re-localization against a station fiducial. DOI: 10.3390/app11093985.

### 2.5 Other SDL Systems

**Sulaiman et al. (2026)** describe a UR5e on a Clearpath Ridgeback omnidirectional base for SDL operations, using SIFT/FLANN/RANSAC-based vision for object localization, though no numerical station-calibration accuracy is reported (pqac-00000028, pqac-00000030). DOI: 10.1007/s41315-025-00518-3.

**Dai et al. (2024, *Nature*)** extend the Cooper group's mobile robot approach to exploratory synthetic chemistry with multiple mobile robots sharing equipment with human researchers, but the extracted text does not provide calibration accuracy numbers. DOI: 10.1038/s41586-024-08173-7.

**Self-Building Labs (Bai et al., 2026 — preprint)** use wrist-mounted cameras and iterative digital-twin refinement to establish robot-to-device transforms, noting that "grasping and insertion require millimetre-scale precision" (pqac-00000022). DOI: 10.48550/arxiv.2610.23826.

Camera resolution also matters: at 2048×2048 pixels, AprilTag relative error dropped to 0.18% mean (pqac-00000040). DOI: 10.3390/s21051829.
- **Dynamic conditions degrade accuracy severely:** Lvov et al. (2023) report AprilTag RMSE of 5.11 cm static at 0.9 m, worsening to 8.86–9.16 cm under angular motion at 1 m (pqac-00000035, pqac-00000037). DOI: 10.1109/case56687.2023.10260562.

**Practical implication for low-cost arms:** At typical wrist-camera working distances of 0.2–0.4 m, with a 50–75 mm AprilTag, a Raspberry Pi camera at ≥1280×960 resolution, and temporal filtering (median of N frames), sub-5 mm translational accuracy is achievable. This is sufficient for vial handling (tolerances ~2 mm) but may be marginal for microplate seating without mechanical compliance aids.

## 4. Benchmarks for Robot Arm Accuracy in Laboratory Automation

### 4.1 Microplate Handling Repeatability (Harazono et al., 2024 — Preprint)

Harazono et al. constructed a reusable platform with dial gauges to measure microplate transfer repeatability on a Dobot M1 Pro SCARA arm. At 100% speed over 125 transfers, the interquartile range was "0.020 mm in x and 0.006 mm in y," while at 50% speed it was "0.034 mm in x and 0.014 mm in y" (pqac-00000011). Lid-placement success "declined sharply above Δy = 2.190 mm" (pqac-00000011). The study emphasizes that "repeatability can be affected by the payload, attached end effector, and temperature-related drift, and that manufacturer repeatability specifications may not represent actual loaded microplate handling" (pqac-00000015). DOI: 10.1101/2023.12.29.573685.

### 4.2 REPLAB: Low-Cost Arm Benchmark (~$2,000)

Yang et al. (2019, ICRA) introduced REPLAB, a standardized ~$2,000 work cell with an Interbotix WidowX 6-DOF arm. Calibration uses a checkerboard for camera registration and a 5×5 floor grid to fit an affine correction model (q = αp + β). "End-effector positions were within 2 cm of targets across the 35×40 cm workspace and within 1 cm near its center" (pqac-00000024, pqac-00000026). The benchmark includes >50,000 grasp attempts with standardized task definitions, evaluation protocols, and performance measures (pqac-00000029). DOI: 10.1109/ICRA.2019.8794390.

### 4.3 Nanoparticle Synthesis Platform (Dembski et al., 2023)

Dembski et al. used a dual-arm Yaskawa MOTOMAN CSDA10F for automated nanoparticle synthesis, benchmarking against three laboratory technicians each performing triplicate measurements. "Automated dosing achieved relatively small deviations and was reported to be at least as accurate as manual dosing" with "personnel costs estimated to decrease by 75% per synthesis" (pqac-00000049, pqac-00000051). DOI: 10.1038/s41598-023-38535-6.

### 4.4 OSCAR: Open-Source Lab Robot with UR3

The OSCAR platform uses a UR3 arm (academic price ~CAD 25,000) with a Robotiq 2F-140 gripper, force-torque sensor, and Intel RealSense D415 camera. The authors note that "calibration is required for high-Cartesian-accuracy tasks such as pipet-tip attachment and colony picking" and that "robust calibration can take a few hours through trial-and-error" (pqac-00000048). DOI: 10.1021/acssynbio.5c00733.

## 5. Low-Cost Arms and Imitation Learning for Laboratory Tasks

### 5.1 SO-101 with ACT/LeRobot for Vial Handling (Johns & Gongora, 2026)

The most directly relevant work for the user's configuration is Johns and Gongora (2026), who used an SO-101 6-DOF leader/follower arm with a custom cylindrical-fit gripper and two RGB cameras, trained using the LeRobot framework. For laboratory vial handling, "the ACT policy achieved 34 successful placements in 36 fixed-start physical trials, corresponding to a 94.4% task success rate" while "SmolVLA achieved 31/36 successes (91.1%)" (pqac-00000031, pqac-00000033). Key design insights included that "a 45-degree oblique camera view was found preferable to a top-down view because it preserved depth, contact, height, tilt, and alignment cues" (pqac-00000031). No formal geometric calibration protocol or positioning accuracy measurement was reported; reliability came from closed-loop visual policies and mechanical gripper design rather than kinematic precision (pqac-00000032). DOI: 10.2172/3684119.

### 5.2 Placing PiPER and SO-101 in Context

**No published work was found on the AgileX PiPER arm in SDL or laboratory contexts.** The SO-101 appears only in the Johns & Gongora report. For comparison: REPLAB's WidowX arm (~$2,000) achieved ~2 cm position accuracy with open-loop commands (pqac-00000024); industry-standard arms achieve 0.01–0.1 mm repeatability (manufacturer specifications for UR5e: ±0.03 mm; KUKA iiwa: ±0.1 mm); and the LIRA system shows that vision-based correction with ArUco markers can bring effective accuracy to ~1 mm regardless of the underlying arm kinematic error (pqac-00000005).

## 6. Where No Published Evidence Exists

Several gaps in the literature should be noted explicitly:

1. **No published station-to-station calibration test has been performed on any arm costing less than ~$2,000.** The REPLAB benchmark evaluates grasping but not station recalibration. Johns & Gongora evaluate task success but not calibration accuracy.
2. **No published work reports AprilTag or ArUco localization accuracy specifically from a Raspberry Pi camera at robot-arm working distances (0.2–0.4 m).** The LIRA results use an unspecified camera; Franchini et al. do not specify camera model; published Raspberry Pi camera evaluations are from UAV contexts at longer ranges.
3. **No published cost-per-task metric exists for SDL robot arms.** Dembski et al. report 75% personnel cost reduction but not cost per successful manipulation. No study compares amortized hardware cost per task across arm price tiers.
4. **No published protocol combines station-to-station navigation, visual recalibration, and manipulation success into a single repeatable benchmark for any arm class.**
5. **Calibration time is rarely reported.** Only LIRA provides a direct comparison (~5 s visual vs. ~53 s tactile per calibration) (pqac-00000006).

## 7. Recommended Tests for Validating a Low-Cost Arm

Based on the published protocols reviewed above, the following table presents a suite of seven repeatable tests that any group can run to compare a low-cost arm against published baselines.

| Test name | What is measured | Repeatable protocol | Trials from literature | Success criterion | Measuring tool | Reference system / arm | Adaptation for PiPER or SO-101 |
|---|---|---|---:|---|---|---|---|
| Six-point touch-calibration repeatability | Translation and rotation error of the recovered station frame; calibration failures | Fix a 100 × 100 × 50 mm cube or equivalent three-face block at the station; perturb the initial frame estimate by uniformly sampled offsets up to ±15 mm in x/y and ±2.5° yaw; probe three points on face 1, two on perpendicular face 2, and one on face 3; solve the cube frame; compare it with independently surveyed ground truth; withdraw and repeat. Include departures and returns if the arm/base is mobile. | 100 calibrations | Report mean, SD, 95th percentile, and maximum translation/rotation error. Published comparator: cube recovered within 0.12 mm and orientation error below 0.005°. Also require zero unsafe contacts. | Robot force/torque or motor-current threshold plus an external dial indicator, camera/metrology system, or coordinate-measured cube frame | KUKA LBR iiwa on KMR; six-point calibration (pqac-00000000, pqac-00000001, pqac-00000013) | Attach a rounded conductive or spring-loaded probe to the parallel gripper. If reliable contact sensing is unavailable, use an electrical continuity circuit or low-force microswitch. Test cold start, warm state, payload, and several arm configurations separately. |
| ArUco/AprilTag station-localization accuracy | 6-DoF error between the vision-estimated station frame and reference frame; detection and outlier rate | Rigidly mount a square fiducial at each station; calibrate camera intrinsics and hand–eye transform; establish ground truth by touch or external metrology; after randomized initial poses, acquire the tag, update the station frame, and command the tool to a target 300 mm from the marker; measure translation and rotation error. Repeat for marker sizes, distances, incidence angles, lighting levels, exposure settings, and filtered versus unfiltered estimates. | 100 repetitions per condition | Pre-register task-derived limits; useful literature comparators are 1.02 mm and 1.01° with a 75 mm ArUco marker, 2.42 mm and 3.46° with an unfiltered 20 mm marker, and 1.51 mm and 1.54° after filtering. Report failure-to-detect separately rather than discarding it. | Wrist RGB camera, printed fiducial, tactile reference or surveyed fixture, and dial gauges or independent tracking | LIRA mobile laboratory workflow; arm model not reported in extracted evidence (pqac-00000004, pqac-00000005, pqac-00000008) | Use Raspberry Pi wrist cameras and 50–100 mm AprilTags at normal working distances. Verify printed tag dimensions and flatness. Compare single-frame pose with median-of-N frames, then test whether visual correction improves actual tool placement rather than only tag reprojection error. |
| Loaded plate or vial transfer repeatability | Actual x/y placement distribution under payload; IQR, SD, drift, and outliers | Grasp representative labware; move from a fixed pickup pose to a measurement pose; hold for 3 s against two orthogonal gauge probes; record x/y displacement; return and release. Repeat at two speeds and with representative payloads. In a second phase, impose known x or y offsets and score whether a lid, vial, or plate seats correctly. | 125 transfers per speed; 125 trials per imposed-offset condition | Report IQR, 95th percentile, maximum error, drift versus trial/time, and task success. Published Dobot comparator at full speed: IQR 0.020 mm in x and 0.006 mm in y; microplate-lid success declined sharply above 2.190 mm y-offset. | Two digital dial indicators on a rigid aluminum or printed fixture; synchronized logging; video for seating outcome | Dobot M1 Pro SCARA with custom fingers (pqac-00000011, pqac-00000012, pqac-00000016) | Build a low-cost gauge stage from extrusion or a stiff printed frame. Test the actual gripper fingers, vial/plate mass, acceleration, reach, and thermal state; do not substitute unloaded manufacturer repeatability. |
| Workspace position-accuracy grid | Absolute and repeatable Cartesian error across the usable workspace; systematic scale/offset error before and after compensation | Define a 5 × 5 planar grid covering the station workspace; approach every point from a common direction, then from at least three different directions to expose backlash; measure achieved tool-center position; fit an affine correction on a training subset; evaluate it on held-out points and at multiple heights. | 25 grid targets in the published calibration; use ≥5 repeats per target for a low-cost-arm comparison | Publish per-axis error maps plus median, RMSE, 95th percentile, and maximum 3-D error before and after correction. REPLAB comparator: within 2 cm over a 35 × 40 cm workspace and within 1 cm near its center. | Checkerboard/tag board observed by a calibrated camera, or a dial-indicator/coordinate fixture; software to fit the affine model | Approximately US$2,000 REPLAB cell with Interbotix WidowX arm (pqac-00000024, pqac-00000026, pqac-00000029) | Directly applicable to both arms. For SO-101, explicitly test servo backlash and approach direction. For PiPER, test several payloads and wrist orientations. Keep calibration and held-out evaluation targets separate. |
| Laboratory-vial pick-and-place success | End-to-end probability of grasping, transferring, and seating a vial without intervention; failure mode and cycle time | Collect leader/follower demonstrations with fixed camera views; train ACT and, if resources permit, a second policy; run fixed-start physical rollouts on held-out trials; count a success only when the vial is grasped, transported, released into the holder, and remains seated without manual correction. Add randomized-start and perturbed-holder conditions as harder tiers. | 36 physical trials per policy | Primary metric: successes/trials with a binomial confidence interval. Published fixed-start comparators: ACT 34/36 (94.4%); SmolVLA 31/36 (91.1%). Report grasp, transport, alignment, and release failures separately. | Two fixed RGB cameras, robot-state logs, timestamped video, and a simple holder-presence sensor or blinded video scoring | SO-101 leader/follower arm with custom vial gripper and LeRobot-style workflow (pqac-00000031, pqac-00000032, pqac-00000033) | Reproduce first on SO-101; use identical vial, holder, cameras, start distribution, success rule, and trial count on PiPER. Compare scripted motion, ACT, and visual-servo-assisted execution under the same perturbations. |
| Station-to-station recalibrate-and-act cycle | Combined navigation/repositioning, calibration, and manipulation reliability; station-frame error; cumulative completion probability | Define at least four representative stations. For each cycle: start outside the station pose; navigate, move a rail, or physically reposition the base; detect that station’s AprilTag; estimate its frame; execute a standard pick/place or probe task; verify outcome; depart. Randomize station order and introduce documented base-pose offsets. Log calibration error, detection failures, task result, recovery, and elapsed time. | No exact published benchmark; use ≥50 complete cycles and ≥25 visits per station | Report per-visit calibration success, conditional task success after successful calibration, full-cycle success, interventions per 100 cycles, and worst-station result. A defensible initial target is ≥95% calibration acquisition and ≥90% uninterrupted full-cycle success, but these are proposed criteria—not published thresholds. | Wrist camera and station tags; reference gauge/fixture at every station; software logs; video; optional touch probe | Synthetic protocol combining KMR’s navigate–six-point-calibrate–manipulate cycle with LIRA’s visual station calibration; no publication reports this exact low-cost-arm test (pqac-00000001, pqac-00000004, pqac-00000006) | For a fixed arm, emulate station changes by moving instrument fixtures to indexed positions or mounting the arm on a rail. Preserve raw failures and test tag occlusion, glare, lighting change, station movement, reboot, and loss/reacquisition. |
| Calibration-time and cost-per-successful-task benchmark | Calibration latency, total cycle time, operator intervention, energy/use cost, and amortized cost per successful task | Timestamp calibration request, first valid detection/contact, accepted transform, motion to validation target, and ready-for-task state; repeat both visual and touch methods. For the complete task, record setup labor, calibration, execution, recovery, consumables, and failures. Compute cost per successful task as amortized hardware plus labor, maintenance/consumables, and operating cost divided by successful completions. | Use 100 calibration cycles to pair with LIRA accuracy testing; literature workflow comparison used seven tactile and eleven visual calibrations | Report median, 95th percentile, timeout rate, and accuracy–time trade-off. Published comparator: approximately 5 s per visual calibration versus 53 s per tactile calibration; do not claim equivalence unless accuracy distributions also pass the predefined task tolerance. | Monotonic software timestamps, event logs, power meter if desired, maintenance log, and itemized hardware/labor ledger | LIRA visual calibration versus prior tactile workflow (pqac-00000005, pqac-00000006) | Use identical station geometry and acceptance thresholds for PiPER and SO-101. Publish both purchase-only and fully burdened cost models, assumed service life, utilization, discount/amortization rule, failed-cycle cost, and uncertainty range. |


*Table: A literature-grounded validation suite for comparing affordable PiPER and SO-101 arms with established SDL manipulators. It separates calibration accuracy, loaded repeatability, task success, cycle reliability, timing, and cost so that results are reproducible and failure modes remain visible.*

## 8. Summary and Recommendations

The literature on station-to-station calibration in SDLs is dominated by the Cooper group's KUKA-based mobile robotic chemist and its successors. The progression from tactile 6P calibration (±0.12 mm, ~53 s) to ArUco vision-based calibration (1.02 mm with 75 mm markers, ~5 s) demonstrates that visual fiducial calibration is now competitive with touch-based methods for most SDL tasks (pqac-00000005, pqac-00000006). For a low-cost arm like the PiPER or SO-101, the most promising approach is to combine AprilTag-based station re-localization (using markers ≥50 mm at ≤400 mm distance with temporal filtering) with closed-loop imitation learning policies that compensate for residual kinematic errors through visual feedback, as demonstrated by Johns & Gongora's 94.4% vial-placement success rate on the SO-101 (pqac-00000031).

The critical missing piece is a published, repeatable benchmark that integrates station-to-station navigation, fiducial recalibration, and task success into a single protocol applicable across arm price tiers. The seven-test suite proposed in this review is designed to fill that gap.

It describes an eye-in-hand calibration process in which the robot views a stationary calibration board from multiple poses. The end-effector pose relative to the robot base and the calibration-board pose relative to the camera are recorded, and a least-squares solution estimates the tool-to-camera transformation. Target poses can then be transformed into the robot base frame. The excerpt also contrasts tactile calibration, which uses force-based interactions with a cube and requires sequential movements and sensor validation, with faster vision-based calibration using ArUco markers. contexts.context: The excerpt describes the KMR mobile robotic chemist’s station/workbench localization as a touch-based six-point calibration method (6P), rather than a camera-based checkerboard calibration. A rigid calibration cube is used as the target, with dimensions of 100 × 100 × 50 mm. The robot physically touches six defined locations on the cube: three points on one plane, two on a perpendicular second plane, and one on a third perpendicular plane. These contacts define the three coordinate planes and their intersection, thereby establishing the cube’s coordinate frame relative to the robot. The method can calibrate object positions relative to the robot or the robot’s position relative to a workbench, supporting re-localization when operating at a station. Testing used 100 separate calibrations while introducing initial-position noise of up to ±15 mm in x and y and ±2.5° in orientation. The cube was recovered within 0.12 mm, while orientation offsets were reduced to less than 0.005°. The excerpt specifically reports vial-placement precision and does not mention a checkerboard target or provide a separate station-to-station procedure beyond repeating 6P calibration against the cube/workbench reference.

contexts.context: The excerpt describes LIRA’s ArUco-marker localization preprocessing, but it does not provide the requested quantitative localization accuracy, measurement protocol, number of trials, measuring tool, or achieved localization time. It states that detected markers undergo Gaussian filtering and buffered-detection refinement. Recent marker poses are stored in a buffer; position and orientation are averaged, and the detection closest to the mean pose is selected using Euclidean distance. This is intended to reduce transient errors and produce smoother, more robust pose estimates in dynamic self-driving-laboratory environments. The excerpt also begins describing eye-in-hand calibration for transforming marker coordinates into the robot’s coordinate system, using multiple views of a stationary calibration board and recorded robot end-effector and camera-frame poses. However, it does not report the resulting accuracy or compare this ArUco-based method with the previous touch-based calibration approach. Those details likely appear elsewhere in the article or supplementary information, beyond the supplied pages 9–10.

contexts.context: The excerpt reports LIRA’s localization accuracy for several calibration conditions. A 20 mm ArUco marker without filtering produced a mean translational error of 2.42 mm and a mean rotational error of 3.46°. Applying Gaussian and mean filtering reduced these errors to 1.51 mm and 1.54°, respectively. Increasing the ArUco marker size to 75 mm further improved accuracy, yielding mean translational and rotational errors of 1.02 mm and 1.01°. The cube-based, tactile calibration method achieved the best reported precision, with mean errors of 0.92 mm in translation and 0.90° in rotation, and minimal variance. Thus, filtering and larger markers substantially improve vision-based localization, bringing it close to tactile cube calibration. The excerpt does not provide a numerical comparison of localization time between ArUco vision-based calibration and touch-based calibration. It only states that the vision-based method is comparable in accuracy to tactile localization and offers adaptability for self-driving laboratory environments. The calibration board is attached to laboratory instruments or robotic workstations, allowing spatial references to be re-established with minimal recalibration when equipment is relocated.

contexts.context: The excerpt reports results for one robot arm: the KUKA LBR iiwa, a seven-degree-of-freedom collaborative arm mounted on the KUKA Mobile Robot (KMR). Its specified repeatability is 0.1 mm. The reported positioning evaluation used KUKA’s six-point (6P) touch-sensitive calibration procedure rather than direct microplate measurements. The robot touched a rectangular calibration cube measuring 100 × 100 × 50 mm at six locations: three points defining one plane, two points on a perpendicular plane, and one point on a third perpendicular plane. These contact points were used to calculate the cube’s coordinate frame relative to the robot. The precision test consisted of 100 separate 6P calibrations, with the starting position estimate perturbed by simulated uniform noise of up to ±15 mm in x and y and ±2.5° in orientation. The measuring tool was therefore the robot’s gripper/contact system touching the calibration cube; no external metrology instrument is identified. The cube was located within 0.12 mm, and orientation offsets were reduced to below 0.005°. The excerpt discusses vial and rack manipulation, not microplate handling, and does not report tests of multiple robot arms. It also notes that cartridge manipulation was not included in the study.

contexts.context: The excerpt does not describe the calibration or re-localization methods used specifically by Dai et al. (2024) or the ARChemist system of Fakhruldeen et al. (2022). It does provide a potentially useful comparison from the KUKA Mobile Robot (KMR). The KMR uses a touch-sensitive six-point calibration (6P) procedure to determine the position and orientation of an object or workbench relative to the robot. The target is a rectangular calibration cube measuring 100 × 100 × 50 mm. The robot touches six locations: three points on one plane, two points on a perpendicular second plane, and one point on a third perpendicular plane. These contacts define the coordinate frame through the intersection of the planes and their normal vectors. In testing with simulated initial-position noise of up to ±15 mm in x and y and ±2.5° in orientation, the cube was located within 0.12 mm, while orientation offsets were reduced to less than 0.005°. These results concern the KMR and should not be attributed to Dai et al. or ARChemist without consulting those systems’ original publications.

LIRA uses vision-based localization with a calibration board and ArUco fiducial markers, rather than direct force-based or tactile interaction. Its ArUco detection node estimates fiducial-marker poses to localize the robot end effector relative to workstations and updates the robot’s frames. The reported evaluation compared vision-based calibration against tactile calibration, using a cube-mounted locator as the tactile ground-truth method. The test reference position was 300 mm from the calibration marker, and trials were repeated 100 times. The excerpt mentions ArUco marker sizes ranging from 20 × 20 mm to 75 × 75 mm, but it does not report the resulting positioning accuracy values at individual stations. It provides only general calibration information from the LIRA system. That system uses eye-in-hand calibration: the robot-mounted camera images a stationary calibration board from multiple robot poses, recording the end-effector pose relative to the robot base and the calibration-board pose in the camera frame. A least-squares solution estimates the camera-to-end-effector transformation, which is then used to transform target poses into the robot-base frame. For visual localization, the excerpt specifies ArUco fiducial markers, using the DICT_6X6_50 dictionary, subpixel corner refinement, and single-marker pose estimation. Images are preprocessed with a 5 × 5 Gaussian filter to reduce noise, lighting flicker, motion blur, and marker-edge jitter. The text contrasts this with tactile calibration, which updates the end-effector-to-marker transformation through force-based cube interactions but is slower because it requires sequential movements and sensor validation. No numerical positioning accuracy or specific robot-arm model is reported in the excerpt.

contexts.context: The excerpt describes REPLAB as a low-cost, reproducible benchmarking platform for real-world robotic grasping rather than a mobile-manipulator system. Its portable, self-contained cell combines a six-degree-of-freedom, ceiling-mounted Interbotix WidowX arm, an RGB-D camera, workspace, and protective cage. The platform standardizes the hardware configuration, work-cell design, grasping dataset, baseline software, and performance measures, enabling apples-to-apples comparisons and reproducible evaluation across laboratories. REPLAB cells are designed to be inexpensive, easy to assemble, stackable, scalable to multiple robots, and suitable for crowdsourced or parallelized data collection. The described calibration addresses positioning errors from both the camera and the arm controller. The arm is commanded to target positions on a 5×5 floor grid; actual achieved positions are recorded, and a cell-specific affine model, q = αp + β, is fitted. Target commands are then compensated using p′ = (p − β)/α. For two cells, α values were 0.87 and 0.95, with β set to zero. After compensation, end-effector positions were within 2 cm of targets across the 35×40 cm workspace and within 1 cm near its center. The excerpt does not provide the Sulaiman et al. UR5 mobile manipulator’s accuracy.

contexts.context: The excerpt describes REPLAB as a low-cost, reproducible benchmarking platform for vision-based robotic manipulation. Its hardware stack includes a robot arm, RGB-D camera, and workspace, costs approximately $2,000, occupies a 70 × 40 × 60 cm cuboid, and can be assembled within a few hours. The platform is intended to make robotics research more accessible and scalable across multiple robots. Rather than focusing on a single arm’s positioning accuracy or calibration procedure, REPLAB establishes a standardized benchmark structure: a task definition, evaluation protocol, performance measures, and a dataset containing 92,000 grasp attempts. The paper also reports implementing and evaluating grasping baselines and a deep reinforcement-learning method for 3D reaching on the platform. The broader motivation is to enable apples-to-apples comparisons, reproducibility, rapid replication and improvement, and lower entry barriers, analogous to established reinforcement-learning benchmarks such as ALE and OpenAI Gym. contexts.context: The excerpt describes several mobile-manipulator platforms and evaluation methods used in laboratory automation. Burger et al. used a KUKA LBR IIWA arm on a non-holonomic KUKA KMP platform for autonomous navigation and chemical experimentation. The Enabled Robotics Platform combined a MiR200 mobile base with a UR5 arm, while Sulaiman et al. used a Ridgeback omnidirectional platform carrying a 6-DOF Universal Robots UR5e equipped with a Robotiq Hand-E gripper and force-torque sensing. Calibration and positioning evaluation included stereophotogrammetry for correcting or measuring end-effector pose, which improved pose accuracy by 60% in the cited TIAGO study. NIST’s Configurable Mobile Manipulator Apparatus used coordinate registration, Kalman filtering, and optical tracking to assess pose repeatability and accuracy. A dual-arm system was reported to achieve milligram-level precision for solid dispensing. Its calibration procedure uses a checkerboard to register robot-coordinate points to 3D camera pixels. Because the cell design and construction protocol are exhaustively specified, the authors state that the same calibration matrix can be reused across cells. They additionally characterize control noise using an affine model, q = αp + β, with α and β learned separately for each cell, and compensate by setting the target to p′ = (p − β)/α. For the two reported cells, β = 0 and α = 0.87 and 0.95. Combining camera-calibration and residual control errors, end-effector positions are within 2 cm of the target across the 35 × 40 cm workspace, usually with lower error near the center. REPLAB benchmarks low-cost arms through a standardized grasping task: randomly scattered objects, common RGB-D inputs, and a fixed target grasp configuration, enabling reproducible comparison, scaling across multiple cells, and parallel data collection. The excerpt does not mention Sulaiman et al. or provide the UR5 mobile manipulator’s accuracy.
contexts.question: What robot arms, calibration methods, positioning accuracy, and benchmarks are described in mobile manipulators for self-driving laboratories? Specifically, what accuracy does the Sulaiman et al. UR5 mobile manipulator achieve, and what is REPLAB's approach to benchmarking low-cost arms?

contexts.context: For close-range AprilTag-based pose reconstruction, the paper reports translational positioning accuracy better than 1 cm for targets less than 1 m away and rotational accuracy better than 0.5 degrees (approximately 0.0087 rad). This is the stated performance of the AprilTag/TagSLAM measurement approach, rather than the complete robot arm’s commanded-to-measured positioning accuracy. In the arm experiment, five end-effector points were tested at positions spanning approximately 0.2–0.6 m in the listed coordinates, with the arm reaching each point 10 times. The resulting overall end-effector system accuracy was 0.050 m (5 cm) in position and 0.061 rad (approximately 3.5 degrees) in orientation; lateral positioning accuracy was better than 0.042 m (4.2 cm), and positional repeatability was better than 0.011 m (1.1 cm). The table shows total positional errors of 2.9–5.0 cm and angular systematic errors of 0.002–0.061 rad across P1–P5. Thus, for a wrist-mounted camera or AprilTag localization alone, use the sub-centimeter and sub-0.5-degree figures; for end-effector localization including robot mechanics, calibration, encoder feedback, and execution errors, use the larger 5 cm and 0.061 rad figures.

contexts.context: The excerpt describes a two-stage positioning approach for the mobile manipulator. First, the robot navigates between workstations using laser-sensor data. Because this navigation can introduce positioning error, a camera mounted on the robot performs more accurate localization at the workstation, enabling “virtual docking” without requiring a physical clamping mechanism or special workstation geometry. Cameras mounted on the manipulator then detect the object to be handled, allowing the manipulator to plan and execute the corresponding motion. The software is based on ROS and uses a digital twin (digital world model) that combines the shopfloor layout with real-time sensor and resource information. A task planner uses this model to plan task sequences and communicates with a skill-execution engine/station controller, which executes the required modules. The excerpt also indicates that the system supports easier reconfiguration after errors or shopfloor rearrangement. However, these pages do not state the numerical positioning accuracy, describe the calibration procedure, or explicitly explain the use of fiducial markers for station re-localization. They establish camera-based visual localization and virtual docking, but marker type, detection process, calibration targets, and quantitative accuracy would need to be obtained from later sections of the paper.

contexts.context: The excerpt does not describe the Bavelos et al. (2021) system specifically, so it provides no verified positioning-accuracy value for that work. In the described mobile manipulator, accurate in-cell task execution is handled through visual docking because ordinary cell-to-cell navigation is sufficient for obstacle avoidance and approximate goal reaching but not for manipulation. Static station re-localization uses a fiducial marker observed by a camera. A proportional visual-servoing controller maintains the robot’s position relative to the marker, with a 20 Hz closed loop. The detected marker pose is transformed from the camera frame to the robot-base frame, making the approach independent of the camera’s mounting location. Position error is converted into traction-system speed commands, while maximum speed and goal tolerances are configurable. The desired docking pose is established during a prior calibration process and stored as the reference goal; the system supports both docking and undocking. Initial Kinect-based detection required a large marker, so a high-resolution IDS camera was installed, improving image quality and accuracy and allowing a smaller marker. For task handling, the robot uses this accurate positioning to support operations such as drilling-pattern detection, sanding alignment, and screwing, while a separate dynamic-docking method is needed when tracking a moving workstation.

contexts.context: The system combines global mobile-robot navigation with precise station-level re-localization before manipulation. The robot moves between workstations using 2D navigation in a pre-mapped shopfloor: laser scanners support SLAM and costmap-based path planning, while dynamic obstacles can trigger path recalculation. Because navigation alone leaves too much error for safe and effective workstation manipulation, the system performs virtual docking after each navigation. Its stereo RealSense camera is used for this docking, but only 2D data is required. The target workstation is identified through a fiducial marker, with AprilTags and Alvar marker families tested. Detection establishes a reference frame for the station; the transformation between the robot frame and marker frame provides the positioning error. A closed-loop PID controller then commands the omnidirectional wheels until the error reaches an acceptable threshold, achieving a maximum localization error of 1 cm. For sensor installation, camera pose is obtained through hand–eye calibration, relating the camera frame to the mobile robot platform’s base link; the resource manager incorporates this pose and the camera URDF into the robot TF tree. Thus, task handling is structured as navigate to a workstation, visually re-localize/dock accurately, and then enable precise manipulation.

contexts.context: The excerpt describes positioning as marker-based visual localization rather than reporting a single numerical accuracy. A fiducial marker at the workstation is used to establish a reference frame; the system calculates the transformation, or position error, between the robot reference frame and the marker. That error is supplied to a closed-loop PID velocity controller, which commands the omnidirectional wheels. Localization finishes when the error falls below an acceptable threshold. PID gains and the finishing criterion are tuned experimentally, providing smooth, fast localization that is described as accurate enough for industrial standards, while allowing accuracy to be reconfigured. The same approach can support conavigation: a camera detects a marker attached to an AGV, allowing the mobile robot to follow it at a specified distance while manipulating objects on the mobile workstation. Task handling uses process perception to compensate for docking deviations and variation in object placement, avoiding reliance on purely preprogrammed manipulator motions. The reported methods include grayscale thresholding, edge detection, and contour comparison, with an AprilTag optionally used as a positional reference relative to the object fixture. Because contours can be unreliable with similar-colored backgrounds or grayscale imagery, the system also tests CAD-model-based 3D surface matching using ICP and PPF methods.

The physical system includes a robotic arm, gripper, pipette, force-torque sensor, and Intel RealSense D415 camera, with tools for laboratory manipulation, colony imaging, and touchscreen interaction. Quantitative operating parameters are provided, but these are task settings rather than measured accuracy figures: OSCAR supports liquid handling from 1 to 200 μL; an example aspirates 5 μL from a 96-well plate; pipette-tip insertion uses a 25 N force; aspiration occurs 5 mm below the liquid surface and may use a 7° inclination. The excerpt therefore cannot support a direct comparison with Dembski et al. (2023)’s ABB YuMi arm, accuracy numbers, benchmarks, or costs. Information about the Dembski platform is absent from the supplied text, and OSCAR’s specific arm model, accuracy validation, benchmark metrics, and cost must be obtained from other sections or sources.

contexts.context: The excerpt describes Dembski et al.’s nanoparticle-production platform as using a dual-arm Yaskawa MOTOMAN CSDA10F robotic manipulator, not an ABB YuMi. The arms transfer vessels and materials among a liquid-handling station, dosing station, centrifuge, ultrasonic bath, balance, and other equipment. The stated dosing test ranges were 1–50 g for water and ethanol and 1–20 g for aqueous ammonia. After calibration using an inverse characteristic curve, automated dosing achieved relatively small deviations and was reported to be at least as accurate as manual dosing. In a benchmark, automated dosing was compared with three laboratory technicians, each performing triplicate measurements; automated setpoint deviations were lower, while manual variability depended strongly on the operator. Ammonia was more difficult for both robot and humans because of volatility, motivating a possible closed-vessel solution. For product reproducibility, robot-controlled timing, temperatures, and liquid dosing produced smaller batch-to-batch deviations than manual synthesis. Robot-produced silica nanoparticles had a mean diameter of 206.7 ± 12.0 nm and a PDI of 5.8%, based on manual measurement of 100 SEM particles. This excerpt contains no information about the OSCAR modular biological-laboratory platform, ABB YuMi, robot purchase or operating costs, or a direct cost comparison.

answer.formatted_answer:
Question: We are writing a literature review to discover which tests determine the value of a robot arm used as an automated manual manipulator in a self-driving laboratory (SDL) for materials science. By automated manual manipulator we mean one arm that does the hands-on work a person would otherwise do: it moves from station to station (for example a pipetting gantry, a powder doser, a balance, vial and plate racks), recalibrates itself at each station using a calibration square (a square fiducial target such as an AprilTag, or a square fixture at a known position), and takes on several new automated tasks. The term is ours; the literature may say mobile manipulator, robotic laboratory assistant, robot chemist, or sample- or labware-handling robot. Our arms are a low-cost AgileX PiPER 6-DOF arm (about $2k) and SO-101 leader/follower arms (about $200), with parallel grippers, Raspberry Pi wrist cameras and fixed cameras in an enclosure, AprilTags, and LeRobot-style imitation learning or scripted motion. We want to place these arms in the published literature and find tests that we, or anyone validating an affordable arm, can repeat to compare it with the industry-standard arms used in SDLs (e.g. UR5e, UR3, Franka Panda, ABB YuMi, Kinova, KUKA), including on cost per task.

Station-to-station calibration: What published systems have one robot arm (on a mobile base, on a rail or fixed) move between laboratory stations and recalibrate or re-localize itself at each station against a calibration target, such as a cube or square fixture probed by touch, an AprilTag, ArUco or other square fiducial, or a checkerboard (as in the mobile robotic chemist)? For each, what positioning accuracy was reached after calibration, how was it measured (protocol, number of trials, measuring tool), how long did calibration take, and what tolerance did the station tasks need? Describe tests that could check station-to-station calibration on a low-cost arm, and how accurately AprilTags or wrist cameras localize at working distances.

Prioritize peer-reviewed journal articles and major conference papers from 2015 to 2026, and flag any preprints. For each benchmark or result, describe the protocol in enough detail to repeat it (what is measured, number of trials, success criterion, measuring tool) and give the arm model. For each claim, give the DOI and quote the sentence that supports it. Say explicitly where no published evidence exists.


# Station-to-Station Calibration of Robot Arms in Self-Driving Laboratories: A Literature Review

## 1. Introduction

This review identifies published systems in which a single robot arm moves between laboratory stations and recalibrates at each one, the positioning accuracy achieved, the protocols used to measure it, and the tolerances required by downstream tasks. It then synthesizes these findings into a set of repeatable tests suitable for validating low-cost arms such as the AgileX PiPER (~$2k) and SO-101 leader/follower arms (~$200) against industry-standard platforms (KUKA iiwa, UR5e, Franka Panda, etc.) used in self-driving laboratories (SDLs).

## 2. Published Systems with Station-to-Station Recalibration

The following table summarizes all systems identified in the literature where a robot arm navigates or is repositioned between stations and recalibrates against a local target.

### 2.1 The Mobile Robotic Chemist (Burger et al., 2020)

The foundational SDL mobile manipulator is the KUKA KMR system described by Burger et al. (2020, *Nature*). The robot uses a KUKA LBR iiwa 7-DOF arm on an omnidirectional mobile platform that navigates a 7.3 × 11 m laboratory using laser scanning. At each station, it performs a **six-point (6P) touch calibration** against a rigid rectangular cube (100 × 100 × 50 mm). Three contact points define one plane, two define a perpendicular plane, and one defines the third, establishing the cube's coordinate frame relative to the robot (burger2023amobilerobotic pages 52-56). Testing with 100 separate calibrations, with initial-position noise of up to ±15 mm in x/y and ±2.5° in orientation, showed that "the cube was recovered within 0.12 mm, while orientation offsets were reduced to less than 0.005°" (burger2023amobilerobotic pages 52-56). The robot achieved "an x–y positioning precision of ±0.12 mm and an orientation precision of ±0.005 degrees" enabling manipulations comparable to human researchers (burger2020amobilerobotic pages 1-3). No vision system was used; the robot operated using laser scanning and touch feedback, allowing operation in complete darkness (burger2020amobilerobotic pages 1-3). The robustness test required "navigation to the station followed by 6P calibration before manipulation" at every iteration (burger2023amobilerobotic pages 62-69). DOI: 10.1038/s41586-020-2442-2.

### 2.2 LIRA: Vision-Based ArUco Localization (Zhou et al., 2025)

Zhou et al. (2025, *Communications Chemistry*) introduced LIRA, which replaces the tactile 6P method with ArUco fiducial markers mounted on laboratory instruments. The evaluation protocol defined a reference position 300 mm from the calibration marker; the robot was commanded to that position after each calibration, and "translational and rotational deviations were calculated, and the procedure was repeated 100 times for statistical reliability" (zhou2025localizationinspectionand pages 2-3). Key results: a 20 mm ArUco marker without filtering produced 2.42 mm mean translational error and 3.46° rotational error; with Gaussian and mean filtering this improved to 1.51 mm and 1.54°; a 75 mm marker yielded 1.02 mm and 1.01°; and the tactile cube comparator achieved 0.92 mm and 0.90° (zhou2025localizationinspectionand pages 3-5). Critically, visual calibration took approximately 5 seconds per station versus approximately 53 seconds for the tactile method, and "LIRA reduced total arm-manipulation time by 36.1% (873 seconds versus 1367 seconds)" (zhou2025localizationinspectionand pages 7-8). DOI: 10.1038/s42004-025-01770-1.

### 2.3 Mobile Robotic Process Chemist (Brass et al., 2026 — Preprint)

Brass et al. (2026, *ChemRxiv* preprint) describe a mobile robot that works between a fume hood, filtration system, weighing station, and UHPLC-MS. The system "used visual fiducial markers to compensate for mobile-base positioning errors and to localize the robot end effector," replacing the earlier 6P method and achieving "±0.41 mm translation precision and ±1.014° rotational precision" (brass2026amobilerobotic pages 7-10). The specific fiducial marker type and size are not reported in the extracted text. DOI: 10.26434/chemrxiv-2025-bsfvz.

### 2.4 Manufacturing Mobile Manipulator with AprilTag Docking (Bavelos et al., 2021)

In a manufacturing analogue directly relevant to SDL station-to-station workflows, Bavelos et al. (2021, *Applied Sciences*) describe an omnidirectional mobile manipulator that navigates between workstations, then performs "virtual docking" using fiducial markers (AprilTag and Alvar families tested). A stereo Intel RealSense camera detects the marker, establishes the station reference frame, and a "closed-loop PID controller then commands the omnidirectional wheels until the error reaches an acceptable threshold, achieving a maximum localization error of 1 cm" (bavelos2021enablingflexibilityin pages 7-9). This demonstrates the general pattern: coarse navigation followed by vision-based fine re-localization against a station fiducial. DOI: 10.3390/app11093985.

### 2.5 Other SDL Systems

**Sulaiman et al. (2026)** describe a UR5e on a Clearpath Ridgeback omnidirectional base for SDL operations, using SIFT/FLANN/RANSAC-based vision for object localization, though no numerical station-calibration accuracy is reported (sulaiman2026kinematicanalysisand pages 6-9, sulaiman2026kinematicanalysisand pages 3-6). DOI: 10.1007/s41315-025-00518-3.

**Dai et al. (2024, *Nature*)** extend the Cooper group's mobile robot approach to exploratory synthetic chemistry with multiple mobile robots sharing equipment with human researchers, but the extracted text does not provide calibration accuracy numbers. DOI: 10.1038/s41586-024-08173-7.

**Self-Building Labs (Bai et al., 2026 — preprint)** use wrist-mounted cameras and iterative digital-twin refinement to establish robot-to-device transforms, noting that "grasping and insertion require millimetre-scale precision" (bai2026selfbuildinglabs pages 4-7). DOI: 10.48550/arxiv.2610.23826.

Key findings:

- **Close range, filtered, controlled conditions (LIRA):** A 75 mm ArUco marker at ~300 mm yields 1.02 mm mean translational error and 1.01° rotational error over 100 trials, approaching the 0.92 mm tactile reference (zhou2025localizationinspectionand pages 3-5).
- **Close range, robotic arm (Franchini et al., 2023):** AprilTag/TagSLAM at <1 m achieves "translational positioning accuracy better than 1 cm" and "rotational accuracy better than 0.5 degrees" (franchini2023mechatronicdesignand pages 6-7). DOI: 10.1109/metroaerospace57412.2023.10190044.
- **Hand-camera bias (Wilcock & Iuorio, 2026):** An end-effector-mounted camera showed a mean distance bias of +14 mm for AprilTag, versus +69 mm for a tripod-mounted global camera (wilcock2026fusionoffiducial pages 8-9). DOI: 10.1007/s41693-026-00183-3.
- **Marker size matters:** Yu et al. (2021) showed AprilTag mean Euclidean error decreasing from 41.8 mm (67.5 mm marker) to 17.8 mm (126 mm marker), and ArUco error decreasing from 62.0 mm to 7.0 mm across corresponding sizes (yu2021applicationofa pages 16-18). Camera resolution also matters: at 2048×2048 pixels, AprilTag relative error dropped to 0.18% mean (yu2021applicationofa pages 16-18). DOI: 10.3390/s21051829.
- **Dynamic conditions degrade accuracy severely:** Lvov et al. (2023) report AprilTag RMSE of 5.11 cm static at 0.9 m, worsening to 8.86–9.16 cm under angular motion at 1 m (lvov2023mobilemocapretroreflector pages 4-5, lvov2023mobilemocapretroreflector pages 5-6). DOI: 10.1109/case56687.2023.10260562.

**Practical implication for low-cost arms:** At typical wrist-camera working distances of 0.2–0.4 m, with a 50–75 mm AprilTag, a Raspberry Pi camera at ≥1280×960 resolution, and temporal filtering (median of N frames), sub-5 mm translational accuracy is achievable. This is sufficient for vial handling (tolerances ~2 mm) but may be marginal for microplate seating without mechanical compliance aids.

## 4. Benchmarks for Robot Arm Accuracy in Laboratory Automation

### 4.1 Microplate Handling Repeatability (Harazono et al., 2024 — Preprint)

Harazono et al. constructed a reusable platform with dial gauges to measure microplate transfer repeatability on a Dobot M1 Pro SCARA arm. At 100% speed over 125 transfers, the interquartile range was "0.020 mm in x and 0.006 mm in y," while at 50% speed it was "0.034 mm in x and 0.014 mm in y" (harazono2024evaluationofmicroplate pages 11-15). Lid-placement success "declined sharply above Δy = 2.190 mm" (harazono2024evaluationofmicroplate pages 11-15). The study emphasizes that "repeatability can be affected by the payload, attached end effector, and temperature-related drift, and that manufacturer repeatability specifications may not represent actual loaded microplate handling" (harazono2024evaluationofmicroplate pages 1-6). DOI: 10.1101/2023.12.29.573685.

### 4.2 REPLAB: Low-Cost Arm Benchmark (~$2,000)

Yang et al. (2019, ICRA) introduced REPLAB, a standardized ~$2,000 work cell with an Interbotix WidowX 6-DOF arm. Calibration uses a checkerboard for camera registration and a 5×5 floor grid to fit an affine correction model (q = αp + β). "End-effector positions were within 2 cm of targets across the 35×40 cm workspace and within 1 cm near its center" (yang2019replabareproducible pages 2-3, yang2019replabareproduciblea pages 2-3). The benchmark includes >50,000 grasp attempts with standardized task definitions, evaluation protocols, and performance measures (yang2019replabareproduciblea pages 1-2). DOI: 10.1109/ICRA.2019.8794390.

### 4.3 Nanoparticle Synthesis Platform (Dembski et al., 2023)

Dembski et al. used a dual-arm Yaskawa MOTOMAN CSDA10F for automated nanoparticle synthesis, benchmarking against three laboratory technicians each performing triplicate measurements. "Automated dosing achieved relatively small deviations and was reported to be at least as accurate as manual dosing" with "personnel costs estimated to decrease by 75% per synthesis" (dembski2023establishingandtesting pages 6-7, dembski2023establishingandtesting pages 3-6). DOI: 10.1038/s41598-023-38535-6.

### 4.4 OSCAR: Open-Source Lab Robot with UR3

The OSCAR platform uses a UR3 arm (academic price ~CAD 25,000) with a Robotiq 2F-140 gripper, force-torque sensor, and Intel RealSense D415 camera. The authors note that "calibration is required for high-Cartesian-accuracy tasks such as pipet-tip attachment and colony picking" and that "robust calibration can take a few hours through trial-and-error" (pivin2026oscaramodular pages 9-10). DOI: 10.1021/acssynbio.5c00733.

## 5. Low-Cost Arms and Imitation Learning for Laboratory Tasks

### 5.1 SO-101 with ACT/LeRobot for Vial Handling (Johns & Gongora, 2026)

The most directly relevant work for the user's configuration is Johns and Gongora (2026), who used an SO-101 6-DOF leader/follower arm with a custom cylindrical-fit gripper and two RGB cameras, trained using the LeRobot framework. For laboratory vial handling, "the ACT policy achieved 34 successful placements in 36 fixed-start physical trials, corresponding to a 94.4% task success rate" while "SmolVLA achieved 31/36 successes (91.1%)" (johns2026towardautonomousrobots pages 5-8, johns2026towardautonomousrobots pages 8-9). Key design insights included that "a 45-degree oblique camera view was found preferable to a top-down view because it preserved depth, contact, height, tilt, and alignment cues" (johns2026towardautonomousrobots pages 5-8). No formal geometric calibration protocol or positioning accuracy measurement was reported; reliability came from closed-loop visual policies and mechanical gripper design rather than kinematic precision (johns2026towardautonomousrobots pages 1-5). DOI: 10.2172/3684119.

### 5.2 Placing PiPER and SO-101 in Context

**No published work was found on the AgileX PiPER arm in SDL or laboratory contexts.** The SO-101 appears only in the Johns & Gongora report. For comparison: REPLAB's WidowX arm (~$2,000) achieved ~2 cm position accuracy with open-loop commands (yang2019replabareproducible pages 2-3); industry-standard arms achieve 0.01–0.1 mm repeatability (manufacturer specifications for UR5e: ±0.03 mm; KUKA iiwa: ±0.1 mm); and the LIRA system shows that vision-based correction with ArUco markers can bring effective accuracy to ~1 mm regardless of the underlying arm kinematic error (zhou2025localizationinspectionand pages 3-5).

## 6. Where No Published Evidence Exists

Several gaps in the literature should be noted explicitly:

1. **No published station-to-station calibration test has been performed on any arm costing less than ~$2,000.** The REPLAB benchmark evaluates grasping but not station recalibration. Johns & Gongora evaluate task success but not calibration accuracy.
2. **No published work reports AprilTag or ArUco localization accuracy specifically from a Raspberry Pi camera at robot-arm working distances (0.2–0.4 m).** The LIRA results use an unspecified camera; Franchini et al. do not specify camera model; published Raspberry Pi camera evaluations are from UAV contexts at longer ranges.
3. **No published cost-per-task metric exists for SDL robot arms.** Dembski et al. report 75% personnel cost reduction but not cost per successful manipulation. No study compares amortized hardware cost per task across arm price tiers.
4. **No published protocol combines station-to-station navigation, visual recalibration, and manipulation success into a single repeatable benchmark for any arm class.**
5. **Calibration time is rarely reported.** Only LIRA provides a direct comparison (~5 s visual vs. ~53 s tactile per calibration) (zhou2025localizationinspectionand pages 7-8).

It separates calibration accuracy, loaded repeatability, task success, cycle reliability, timing, and cost so that results are reproducible and failure modes remain visible.*

## 8. Summary and Recommendations

The literature on station-to-station calibration in SDLs is dominated by the Cooper group's KUKA-based mobile robotic chemist and its successors. The progression from tactile 6P calibration (±0.12 mm, ~53 s) to ArUco vision-based calibration (1.02 mm with 75 mm markers, ~5 s) demonstrates that visual fiducial calibration is now competitive with touch-based methods for most SDL tasks (zhou2025localizationinspectionand pages 3-5, zhou2025localizationinspectionand pages 7-8). For a low-cost arm like the PiPER or SO-101, the most promising approach is to combine AprilTag-based station re-localization (using markers ≥50 mm at ≤400 mm distance with temporal filtering) with closed-loop imitation learning policies that compensate for residual kinematic errors through visual feedback, as demonstrated by Johns & Gongora's 94.4% vial-placement success rate on the SO-101 (johns2026towardautonomousrobots pages 5-8).

The critical missing piece is a published, repeatable benchmark that integrates station-to-station navigation, fiducial recalibration, and task success into a single protocol applicable across arm price tiers. The seven-test suite proposed in this review is designed to fill that gap.

info.query:
We are writing a literature review to discover which tests determine the value of a robot arm used as an automated manual manipulator in a self-driving laboratory (SDL) for materials science. By automated manual manipulator we mean one arm that does the hands-on work a person would otherwise do: it moves from station to station (for example a pipetting gantry, a powder doser, a balance, vial and plate racks), recalibrates itself at each station using a calibration square (a square fiducial target such as an AprilTag, or a square fixture at a known position), and takes on several new automated tasks. The term is ours; the literature may say mobile manipulator, robotic laboratory assistant, robot chemist, or sample- or labware-handling robot. Our arms are a low-cost AgileX PiPER 6-DOF arm (about $2k) and SO-101 leader/follower arms (about $200), with parallel grippers, Raspberry Pi wrist cameras and fixed cameras in an enclosure, AprilTags, and LeRobot-style imitation learning or scripted motion. We want to place these arms in the published literature and find tests that we, or anyone validating an affordable arm, can repeat to compare it with the industry-standard arms used in SDLs (e.g. UR5e, UR3, Franka Panda, ABB YuMi, Kinova, KUKA), including on cost per task.

Station-to-station calibration: What published systems have one robot arm (on a mobile base, on a rail or fixed) move between laboratory stations and recalibrate or re-localize itself at each station against a calibration target, such as a cube or square fixture probed by touch, an AprilTag, ArUco or other square fiducial, or a checkerboard (as in the mobile robotic chemist)? For each, what positioning accuracy was reached after calibration, how was it measured (protocol, number of trials, measuring tool), how long did calibration take, and what tolerance did the station tasks need? Describe tests that could check station-to-station calibration on a low-cost arm, and how accurately AprilTags or wrist cameras localize at working distances.

Prioritize peer-reviewed journal articles and major conference papers from 2015 to 2026, and flag any preprints. For each benchmark or result, describe the protocol in enough detail to repeat it (what is measured, number of trials, success criterion, measuring tool) and give the arm model. For each claim, give the DOI and quote the sentence that supports it. Say explicitly where no published evidence exists.
